prose.summary: The steel building structures meet the rule of origin, so the CEPA rate (the reduced rate under the India‑UAE CEPA) can be claimed. The estimated saving is 10000.00 AED. See the checklist below for the required steps.
prose.classification: The product is classified under tariff line 73089090, Other structures of iron or steel, with high confidence. Confirm the code with Indian customs or a customs broker before shipping.
prose.duty: Under the India‑UAE CEPA, the normal (MFN) rate is 15% (effective 10%) and the CEPA rate is 0%. The estimated saving is 10000.00 AED.
prose.origin: The rule of origin requires a change in tariff subheading (CTSH) and at least 40% value addition (VA). CTSH means each non‑originating input must be classified in a different six‑digit subheading than the product, and VA is the share of the product’s price that does not come from non‑originating materials, calculated on an FOB basis. The final manufacturing step took place in the UAE and the work exceeds the minimal operations, which are the simple operations that the agreement says never give origin on their own, so both checks are satisfied. All non‑originating inputs are classified outside subheading 730890, meeting CTSH, and the value addition is 45.0%, above the 40% threshold.

notes.text: Originating materials from India used in production in the UAE may be counted as originating; the final production step in the UAE must still exceed the minimal operations.
The agreement refers to box 8, but India's certificate form uses box 9; India's form determines the entry.
The tariff schedule prints 15%, but an exemption notification lowers the duty actually charged to 10%; the effective rate is used.
Estimate on the shipment value given. India charges duty on the assessable (CIF) value at import, so actual amounts will differ. Shown in the shipment's own currency; never converted.
CEPA rates reduce Basic Customs Duty (BCD) only. IGST, GST compensation cess, SWS and any anti-dumping or safeguard duty still apply.
The CEPA rate applies only if the product qualifies under the rules of origin and a valid certificate of origin is presented.
'+' in a rule is read as 'and' (both tests must pass). The agreement does not define '+', so this is Mansha's interpretation.
Operations and final manufacture are the exporter's own declaration.
'Direct labour cost' and 'direct overhead cost' are not defined in the agreement.
The agreement does not say whether the build-down and build-up methods use the same threshold, apart from the 5-point Ex-Works adjustment.
Interpretation: de minimis helps only the tariff-shift part of a rule, not the VA percentage.

Cumulation is bilateral only: originating materials from India used in production in the UAE may be counted as originating. The last production process in the UAE must still go beyond the minimal operations.
An invoice issued by a third party does not by itself cause the claim to be denied; the exporter must indicate 'third-party invoicing'.
The agreement says box 8, but India's origin rules and certificate form say box 9; India's form governs entry into India.
UAE law sets a shorter 3-year minimum; the CEPA's 5 years governs CEPA claims.

No official page read names the Ministry of Foreign Trade as the issuer of the India CEPA certificate specifically: its service page covers preferential certificates in general, and the India-specific page is still on moet.gov.ae.
Fee bands are in AED and apply to the invoice value in AED; no currency conversion is done by Mansha.

Inference: a producer in a free zone is likely not eligible for Factory Registration, because it requires a factory outside a free zone, and registration is needed before applying for the certificate of origin for India. Confirm with the Ministry of Economy and Tourism.
A product that only undergoes the minimal operations listed in Art. 3.5.1 (a) to (q) does not originate, even if it meets its product-specific rule.
Inference: SWS is charged on the reduced BCD (no CEPA-specific text found).
Inference: anti-dumping and safeguard duties still apply (no exemption found).

That electronic certificates are accepted and uploaded to India's e-Sanchit system comes from CBIC Instruction 28/2022, which Mansha has read only through secondary reports (LiveLaw, taxmann), not the official text.
